description:
We’re putting together a team of six people who are interested in space and enjoy building things. Right now, we’re planning to take on Lunar Landing Site Navigator. Our interests include AI/ML, web development, data visualization, design, and planetary science.

We’d like to meet people with some technical experience who are excited to contribute and learn about new areas. We’re looking for teammates who share ideas, help each other, and want to build something useful together.
summary: Noctis Horizon is a web application that answers one question for any lunar landing site and date: when will a lander have sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication? Users pick one of 19 catalogued sites (Apollo, CLPS, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM and the Artemis III candidate regions near the south pole) or enter any coordinates and dates. The backend requests Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons for an observer standing on the lunar surface and checks them against a real skyline computed from LRO LOLA topography out to 200 km, including lunar curvature. The result is a green, yellow or red verdict with plain-language reasons, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, visibility timelines, a sky panorama, a 3D view of the terrain, a landing-date calendar and a side-by-side comparison of up to four scenarios. At the south pole, moving a site by a few kilometres or slipping a launch by two weeks can decide whether a mission works. The data to check this exists, but it is spread across specialist tools. Noctis Horizon puts it on one screen for mission planners, educators and the public.
details:
What it does

Noctis Horizon helps compare lunar landing sites and dates by power and communication. For a chosen site and time range it shows where the Sun and the Earth are in the local sky, checks them against the real skyline, and reports how long a lander has sunlight, a direct link to Earth, and both at once.

Main features

  • Site catalog and custom input: 19 catalogued sites (Apollo, CLPS missions IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost, Chang'e, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, the south pole, Shackleton, Mons Mouton and Mons Malapert), or any coordinates and any date range from hours to years.
  • Mission verdict: green, yellow or red with plain-language reasons, for two mission types: "Day only" (a lander that works through one stretch of daylight) and "Through the night" (a lander that must survive the lunar night).
  • Metrics and countdowns: share of time sunlit, with Earth in view and with both; the longest stretch with both; the longest night; the longest gap without Earth; time remaining until sunset, Earthset or the end of the power-and-link window.
  • Sky panorama and timeline: the skyline silhouette with the Sun's and Earth's paths, elevation curves and visibility lanes, with playback of the lunar day.
  • Landing-date calendar: the same mission landed on every date for the next 3, 6 or 12 months, coloured by verdict, so a team can see which dates still work after a launch slip.
  • Comparison: up to four scenarios side by side, and a "Better spots nearby" map that runs the same calculation on a grid around the site.
  • Mission Control: a 3D view that starts from the whole Moon, flies down to the site, lands on LOLA terrain, traces 720 skyline rays and then plays the lunar day with lines of sight to the Sun and the Earth. When terrain hides one of them, the line stops on the blocking ridge with its distance and direction.
  • Landing search: scans an 80 km region around the south pole for slope, sunlight, Earth contact and hydrogen, shows the candidates on a LOLA hillshade map from NASA Moon Trek, and reports when no site passes the limits.
  • For educators and the public: a hands-free demo mode, quick starts, a glossary and hints on every metric.

Lunar South Pole, 15 November - 14 December 2026: verdict, metrics, countdowns, sky panorama with the real skyline, and the visibility timeline.

How it works

  1. Ephemerides. For each new scenario the backend queries the JPL Horizons API for the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and the Earth seen from a point on the lunar surface. Libration and orbital geometry are included. The Moon has no atmosphere, so no refraction is applied. Responses are cached.
  2. Skyline. From a point 2 m above the ground, rays are cast every 0.5 degrees of azimuth out to 200 km across the LOLA south polar grid (120 m per pixel, 75-90 S). Terrain samples are placed in 3D on the 1737.4 km sphere, so lunar curvature is handled directly. At the Shackleton - de Gerlache ridge an LROC NAC terrain model with 3.5 m pixels refines the local surface.
  3. Visibility. The Sun is treated as a 0.27 degree disc and counts as up while its upper limb clears the skyline; the Earth counts as in view while its centre clears it. Window edges are interpolated between samples.
  4. Verdict and calendar. Metrics are summarised into the verdict; the calendar reuses one ephemeris and one skyline for the whole span.

Checks against known facts

  • Shackleton's floor comes out at about -2.8 km and receives no sunlight, as expected for a permanently shadowed region.
  • Apollo 11 gets a lunar day of about 14.8 days.
  • Mons Malapert keeps Earth in view through the tested month.

Example result

One lunar day, 15 November - 14 December 2026, hourly step, LOLA terrain, day-only mission:

  • Lunar South Pole (Shackleton rim): sunlight 75%, Earth in view 46%, Sun and Earth together 46%, longest darkness 7.5 days, longest gap without Earth 13.9 days.
  • Mons Malapert: sunlight 55%, Earth in view 100%, Sun and Earth together 55%, longest darkness 12.4 days.
  • IM-1 Odysseus site: sunlight 43%, Earth in view 100%, Sun and Earth together 43%, longest darkness 12.9 days.

The south pole site gets the most light but loses Earth for almost two weeks. Mons Malapert and the IM-1 site never lose Earth, but get less sunlight. All three are viable for a day-only mission; the trade-off between them is exactly what a planner needs to see.

Side-by-side comparison of three polar sites on the same dates. The best value in each row is highlighted.

Benefits and intended impact

When hardware delays or launch slips force a change, planners need to see quickly which nearby site or which new date still gives enough power and contact. Today this means combining several specialist tools and raw tables. Noctis Horizon gives the answer in one screen in seconds, and the same views let teachers and the public see why a few kilometres or a couple of weeks matter so much at the lunar south pole.

Creativity

The verdict is explained, not only computed: in Mission Control the user watches the rays find the skyline and sees the exact ridge that hides the Sun or the Earth, with its distance and direction. The calendar turns "the launch slipped" into a colour map of dates that still work.

Mission Control at the Lunar South Pole: the lander on LOLA terrain, skyline rays and lines of sight to the Sun and the Earth.

NASA data and how we use it

  • JPL Horizons API (challenge resource): apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and the Earth seen from the landing site, for every scenario and every calendar date.
  • NASA Moon Trek (challenge resource): LOLA south polar hillshade tiles under the landing-search candidate map.
  • LRO LOLA polar DEM, 120 m (PDS Geosciences Node): skylines out to 200 km, terrain for the 3D scene and slopes for the landing search.
  • LROC NAC terrain model, 3.5 m: detailed terrain and skyline at the Shackleton - de Gerlache ridge.
  • Lunar Prospector hydrogen map: the resources term of the landing-search score.
  • NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LROC colour, LOLA relief): the globe in Mission Control and the Moon on the Home page.
  • NSSDC and LROC: coordinates of the Apollo and recent landing sites in the catalog.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, TanStack Query, three.js with React Three Fiber and drei.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, httpx, NumPy, Rasterio, Pillow.
  • Testing and quality: Vitest, pytest, Oxlint, Ruff, Prettier, GitHub Actions CI.
  • Deployment: Docker and Nginx on our own server.

Factors we considered and limitations

  • Real skylines exist only south of 75 S, where the polar DEM is; elsewhere the horizon is a smooth sphere, and the app says so.
  • The 120 m grid smooths terrain near the lander; boulders and small craters are not included.
  • Artemis III candidate regions are represented by the centres of their named features, not by precise landing ellipses.
  • Shadows in the 3D view use terrain within 20 km; the verdict always uses the full 200 km skyline.
  • The verdict reflects geometric visibility only; there is no thermal, battery or link-budget model.
